note: Module checks and final check for the Level 2 Mould Remediation pilot (GP-658). Original CARSI questions; no standard text. SME review required before seeding.

questions.questionText: You find staining on the back of a plasterboard sheet behind a vanity. What does that tell you?
questions.explanation: Staining on the back of the board means growth has colonised the material itself. Cleaning the face leaves it behind, so the board is removed under control. It says nothing about whether the leak has stopped.

questions.questionText: Roughly what affected area does this course treat as a Level 2 job?
questions.explanation: This course frames Level 2 as roughly 1–10 m² in a home or small building. Much larger areas are an escalation trigger and are scoped as large-loss work.

questions.questionText: Which material is most likely to be colonised right through when it stays wet?
questions.explanation: Paper-faced plasterboard holds water and feeds mould, so growth goes through it. Tile and glass are non-porous: growth stays on the surface and can be cleaned.

questions.questionText: Under the WHS laws, who must eliminate or minimise the risks on a mould job?
questions.explanation: The person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) running the job holds the primary duty to eliminate risks so far as is reasonably practicable, or minimise them.

questions.questionText: Which control sits highest on the hierarchy of controls for a mould job?
questions.explanation: Fixing the water and removing the colonised material eliminates the hazard, the top of the hierarchy. Signs and a SWMS are administrative controls and a respirator is PPE, the last line.

questions.questionText: The model biological-hazards code was published by Safe Work Australia. When is it enforceable?
options: Only where a state or territory approves
Only on commercial buildings over 1000 m²
Everywhere from the day it was published
Never, because all codes are only suggestions
questions.explanation: A model code becomes enforceable in a jurisdiction only when that jurisdiction approves it. Check your own regulator, and treat the code as good practice everywhere.

questions.questionText: A wardrobe lining in a house renovated in the 1980s looks like flat fibre sheet. What do you do?
options: Stop work and arrange asbestos sampling first
Paint over it and leave it alone
Spray it with water and then remove
Cut it carefully with a shrouded saw
questions.explanation: Asbestos was banned from 31 December 2003, so assume any home built or renovated before 2003 contains it. Do not cut, drill or break a suspect sheet: stop and have it identified by a competent or licensed person.

questions.questionText: An occupant asks whether the mould caused her child's cough. What is the right response?
questions.explanation: You are not a doctor and you do not diagnose. Say what you found and recommend the occupant talks to their GP about any health concerns.

questions.questionText: Which finding is an escalation trigger rather than normal Level 2 work?
questions.explanation: Growth in the air-conditioning system or ducts is an escalation trigger: isolate the system and escalate. The other findings are typical Level 2 scope items.

questions.questionText: A thermal camera shows a cold patch on a ceiling. What should you do next?
questions.explanation: A thermal camera shows temperature differences, not water. Treat a cold patch as a question and confirm with a moisture meter before drawing any conclusion.

questions.questionText: Spotting is spread across cold ceilings near external walls in winter. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Spotting spread across cold surfaces, worst in winter and in poorly ventilated rooms, is the condensation pattern. A leak usually gives one area spreading from a point.

questions.questionText: Room air is 13 °C and 85% RH. A ceiling reads 11 °C. What does that suggest?
questions.explanation: At 13 °C and 85% RH the dew point is about 10.5 °C. A surface at 11 °C is only 0.5 °C above it, so condensation is likely on colder nights.

questions.questionText: What is a dry reference reading?
options: Same material read in an unaffected area
A reading taken after the job ends
A reading taken on the hottest day
The number printed on the meter box
questions.explanation: A dry reference is the same material, read with the same meter and mode, in a part of the building that was not affected. It becomes the drying goal for that material.

questions.questionText: Inside the drying area the g/kg is falling and is lower than the rest of the house. What does that show?
options: A new leak has started nearby
The dehumidifier is removing the water
The air movers need switching off
The readings are not worth recording
questions.explanation: Falling g/kg inside the drying area, lower than the rest of the house, shows water vapour is being removed. If it does not fall, look for an open door, a fresh leak or too little equipment.

questions.questionText: Why read the same numbered points on every visit?
options: It makes the job file much shorter
It means you take fewer readings overall
It shows the trend at each spot
It keeps the client out of rooms
questions.explanation: Reading the same points each visit shows how each spot is drying over time. That trend, against the dry reference, is the evidence that the area reached the goal.

questions.questionText: You have not opened the wall yet. How should the scope describe the affected area?
questions.explanation: Give your best measured estimate and say it will be confirmed after opening up. That keeps the scope honest and lets the assessor see why the area may change.

questions.questionText: In what order should a Level 2 scope be written?
questions.explanation: Writing the scope in work order (area, containment, air, removal, cleaning, drying, verification, waste) lets another technician do the job from it and an assessor check it.

questions.questionText: Plasterboard at 10 mm weighs about 7 kg per m². Roughly how much does 2.43 m² weigh?
questions.explanation: 2.43 m² × 7 kg/m² = 17.0 kg. Estimating weight in the scope lets you plan bag numbers and safe lifting.

questions.questionText: Before building containment, what should you do with the air-conditioning in the area?
options: Leave it running on fan only
Turn it off, seal the vents
Turn it to maximum cooling mode
Remove the indoor unit completely first
questions.explanation: Turn off and isolate the air-conditioning and seal supply and return vents first. A running system can carry spores from the work area through the house.

questions.questionText: Under negative air, how should the film walls of a good containment behave?
options: Draw gently into the work area
Flap loudly in the moving air
Stay perfectly flat and completely still
Bulge outwards into the next room
questions.explanation: Under negative air the walls draw gently inwards. Walls bulging outwards or flapping mean a problem with the seal, the exhaust or the airflow.

questions.questionText: What is the airlock used for on a Level 2 job?
questions.explanation: Workers remove outer PPE in the airlock before stepping into clean areas, and waste bags are cleaned there. It keeps contamination inside.

questions.questionText: A containment is 17.28 m³ and the plan sets 6 air changes per hour. How much air is needed?
questions.explanation: 17.28 m³ × 6 air changes per hour = 103.7, about 104 m³/h. The method is volume × air changes.

questions.questionText: Why plan on less airflow than the number on the scrubber plate?
options: Plates always show double the airflow
The plate shows the machine price
Loaded filters and ducting cut airflow
Australian power runs machines more slowly
questions.explanation: Plate ratings use a clean filter and no ducting. A loaded filter, long ducts and bends cut real airflow, sometimes by half, so plan on the real figure.

questions.questionText: Smoke from a smoke pencil drifts out of the containment at the door flap. What do you check first?
questions.explanation: Smoke drifting out means air is leaving the work area. Check in order: gaps in the film, a kinked or disconnected exhaust duct, a loaded pre-filter, and a door opened elsewhere.

questions.questionText: Which respirator does WA Health recommend for mould removal above about 1 m²?
options: No respirator if the room's ventilated
A paper nuisance-dust mask from hardware
PAPR, or P3 full-face or hood
A loose cloth face mask only
questions.explanation: WA Health's February 2024 indoor mould guidance recommends a powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) for mould removal above about 1 m², or a P3 respirator with a full face or hood where a PAPR is not available. A tight-fitting P2 is the minimum only for small work, and every tight-fitting respirator needs a fit test.

questions.questionText: A technician has a beard and is issued a tight-fitting half-face respirator. What is the problem?
options: Facial hair stops the mask sealing
Beards make respirators far too warm
The cartridges will expire much sooner
There is no problem with this
questions.explanation: A tight-fitting respirator only works if it seals to the face. Facial hair under the seal stops it sealing, so the wearer needs a clean shave or a loose-fitting powered respirator.

questions.questionText: When leaving the work area, which item of PPE comes off last, after leaving the airlock?
questions.explanation: Outer gloves, coveralls and overshoes come off in the airlock. The respirator comes off last, after leaving the airlock, so you are not breathing contaminated air while removing dirty layers.

questions.questionText: An air scrubber draws 2.5 A, a dehumidifier 4.5 A and two air movers 1.2 A each. What is the total?
questions.explanation: 2.5 + 4.5 + 1.2 + 1.2 = 9.4 A. That is too close to a 10 A circuit once motors start, so split the load across two circuits.

questions.questionText: A worker in containment on a hot day becomes dizzy and confused. What do you do?
options: Turn the air scrubber up higher
Give them an energy drink now
Finish the task first, then rest
questions.explanation: Dizziness and confusion are warning signs of heat illness. Stop work, cool the person and call 000 if symptoms are severe.

questions.questionText: A worker is seriously injured on a mould job. Under the WHS laws, what must happen?
options: Record it in the diary only
Notify the regulator, preserve the site
Clean up and carry on working
Tell the insurer next week sometime
questions.explanation: A serious injury is a notifiable incident. Notify the regulator immediately and keep the site undisturbed, except to help someone or make it safe, until the regulator says otherwise.

questions.questionText: Colonised paper-faced plasterboard behind a kitchen cabinet should be:
questions.explanation: Paper-faced plasterboard is porous. When it is colonised, growth is inside it, so it is removed and bagged inside the containment.

questions.questionText: How is mould on sound structural timber framing usually dealt with?
options: The frame is always replaced completely
Painted with sealer straight away instead
HEPA vacuum, brush or sand, wipe
Left alone because timber is safe
questions.explanation: Mould on framing is mostly on and near the surface. HEPA vacuum, then wire brush or HEPA-shrouded sand, then damp wipe. Soft or rotten timber is a builder's call.

questions.questionText: Why should you not break plasterboard over your knee or drop it on the floor?
questions.explanation: Every impact releases spores and fragments. Cut slowly along scored lines and lower pieces straight into a bag inside the containment.

questions.questionText: What is the cleaning sequence for surfaces that stay?
options: HEPA vacuum, damp wipe, dry, HEPA vacuum
Air mover, then HEPA vacuum, then fog
Bleach, then rinse, then the air mover
Damp wipe, then bleach, then paint it
questions.explanation: HEPA vacuum first, then damp wipe with detergent, let it dry, then HEPA vacuum again, then check with a raking torch.

questions.questionText: Why is bleach not the answer for mouldy porous materials?
options: It smells much too strongly indoors
It does not reach growth inside
It costs far too much money
It is banned everywhere in Australia
questions.explanation: Bleach does not reach growth inside porous materials and does not remove dead mould, which can still cause reactions. That is why porous material is removed and surfaces are physically cleaned.

questions.questionText: In which direction do you clean a work area?
options: Top to bottom, clean to dirty
Exit first, then the far wall
Bottom to top, dirty to clean
Left to right, in any order
questions.explanation: Clean from top to bottom so falling dust lands on surfaces not yet cleaned, and from the cleanest part towards the dirtiest, finishing near the exit.

questions.questionText: What stops mould coming back after remediation?
questions.explanation: Mould returns when moisture returns. Removal and cleaning take away the growth; fixing the water and drying the structure stop it returning. No product replaces those steps.

questions.questionText: When may a coating or sealer go on cleaned framing?
options: Before any of the removal starts
After clean, dry framing is verified
Instead of doing the HEPA vacuuming
While the timber is still wet
questions.explanation: Coatings go on only once the structure is clean and dry and verification has passed. Over growth or on wet timber they hide the problem and trap moisture.

questions.questionText: A label says 20 mL per litre. How much concentrate makes 250 mL of solution?
questions.explanation: 0.25 L × 20 mL per litre = 5 mL of concentrate. Always take the dilution from the label.

questions.questionText: When should air movers be switched on in a mould work area?
options: Only while cutting out the plasterboard
Before any of the removal starts
Never at all on mould jobs
After removal and cleaning are done
questions.explanation: While visible growth is present, air movers blow spores around. They stay off until the colonised material is out and surfaces are cleaned, then drying starts inside containment.

questions.questionText: A dehumidifier plate says 50 L/day. In a 21 °C kitchen it removes 9 L on day 1. Why?
options: Plate ratings use warmer, wetter conditions
Australian power is far too weak
The machine must be broken now
The tank was never emptied overnight
questions.explanation: Plate ratings are measured at warm, humid test conditions such as 30 °C and 80% RH. In a cooler room a dehumidifier removes less, so track what it actually removes.

questions.questionText: When is the structure ready to release to verification?
options: After exactly three days of drying time
When the room smells a bit better
When every point holds at the goal
When the builder says they are available
questions.explanation: Drying is finished when every moisture point reaches the goal and stays there on the next reading. Then verification, and only after verification the builder.

quizzes.title: Level 2 Mould Remediation — Final check: Level 2 Mould Remediation

questions.questionText: What is a goose-neck seal?
options: Fold the top once and leave it
Tie a loose knot in the top
Twist the neck, fold it, tape it
Staple the top of the bag shut
questions.explanation: Twist the neck of the bag, fold it over and tape it. It gives a seal that will not open when the bag is carried.

questions.questionText: Where is the outside of a waste bag cleaned before it leaves?
questions.explanation: In the airlock, HEPA vacuum and damp wipe the outside of the bag, then put it in a second clean bag and seal it. Nothing leaves the containment dirty on the outside.

questions.questionText: You paused work because of suspect asbestos. Can that material go in the mould waste bags?
questions.explanation: Asbestos waste is never mixed with mould waste. It is handled under asbestos rules by people licensed or competent to do so.

questions.questionText: Your crew says the room looks clean. Is that the clearance?
options: Yes, a visual check is enough
Yes, if the client agrees too
Yes, if photos are taken too
No, it is your check only
questions.explanation: Looking clean is your crew's own post-remediation check. Verification, ideally by an independent professional, confirms the area is back to normal, and the clearance is the written result.

questions.questionText: Who should verify a job with a newborn returning to the room?
questions.explanation: With a vulnerable occupant, verification should be done by an independent indoor environmental professional who was not involved in the remediation.

questions.questionText: Verification fails. What happens to the containment?
options: It is replaced with new film
It moves into the next room
It stays up while you re-clean
It comes down straight away, today
questions.explanation: Keep the containment and air scrubber in place until verification passes. If it fails, clean again and re-verify.

questions.questionText: Which job-file note is most useful months later?
questions.explanation: Measured facts with photo references answer questions months later. Vague notes do not.

questions.questionText: The cause is a shower seal outside your scope. What do you do at handover?
questions.explanation: If the cause is a maintenance or building issue outside your work, say so plainly and in writing at handover, and keep the note in the file.

questions.questionText: When should the job file be built?
questions.explanation: Build the job file as you go. Records made at the time are accurate and are the evidence if the job is questioned.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between Level 1 and Level 2 mould work?
questions.explanation: Level 2 starts when growth has colonised the material itself, which changes the scope and the controls.

questions.questionText: Put these in order: drying, removal, verification, containment.
questions.explanation: Containment goes up first, then removal and cleaning, then drying to the goal, then verification. Containment stays until verification passes.

questions.questionText: Which is the best evidence that drying is working?
options: Litres, g/kg and readings all falling
The client says it feels drier
The air movers are running loudly
The room smells of cleaning product
questions.explanation: Falling daily litres removed, falling g/kg in the work area and readings moving towards the goal together show drying is working.

questions.questionText: A tight-fitting respirator has not been fit tested on the wearer. What does that mean?
options: It only works outdoors from now
Its protection cannot be relied on
It still protects them fully anyway
It must be worn upside down
questions.explanation: Without a fit test for that wearer on that respirator, you cannot rely on the seal, so you cannot rely on the protection.

questions.questionText: A homeowner asks you to fog the whole house instead of removing a mouldy wall. Your answer?
options: Agree, but charge extra for it
Explain removal and drying solve it
Refuse to do any work there
Agree, because fogging replaces the removal
questions.explanation: Fogging does not remove growth inside materials and adds a chemical exposure. Explain that removal, cleaning, fixing the water and drying do the work.

questions.questionText: Where does the air scrubber exhaust ideally go on a residential job?
questions.explanation: The best exhaust point is outside the building through a window sealed around the ducting. Exhausting into the house risks moving contaminated air into occupied areas.
